name: Course-Specific AI Tutors
title: Course-Specific AI Tutors
answer: Course-specific AI tutors are software systems built or configured for a single course, using the course syllabus, readings, assignments, and instructor guidance to answer student questions and give feedback. They differ from general chatbots because their knowledge is limited to the course materials and their responses are shaped by the instructor's teaching goals. The scope includes question answering, worked examples, practice problems, and feedback on drafts or code, but not grading that replaces the instructor's judgment. These tutors sit inside a learning management system or a separate course site, and they are used by enrolled students during a term.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Course-specific AI tutors are software systems built or configured for a single course, using the course syllabus, readings, assignments, and instructor guidance to answer student questions and give feedback. They differ from general chatbots because their knowledge is limited to the course materials and their responses are shaped by the instructor's teaching goals. The scope includes question answering, worked examples, practice problems, and feedback on drafts or code, but not grading that replaces the instructor's judgment. These tutors sit inside a learning management system or a separate course site, and they are used by enrolled students during a term.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A course-specific tutor usually runs on a hosted large language model accessed through an application programming interface, with a retrieval layer that searches the course's uploaded documents. The course materials are stored as text chunks in a vector database, and the tutor retrieves relevant passages before generating an answer. The system needs a student identity check through the institution's single sign-on, a chat interface, and a log of interactions for the instructor to review. Compute is modest for a single course, but costs rise with the number of students and the length of the course.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The tutor is built by uploading the syllabus, lecture notes, readings, and assignment prompts, then writing a system prompt that tells the model to answer only from those sources and to admit when it does not know. Instructors often add sample question and answer pairs to show the desired tone and level of detail. The retrieval step finds the most relevant course passages and passes them to the model with the student's question, a method called retrieval augmented generation. The tutor is tested on past exam questions or common student misunderstandings before it is released to a class.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main rights and risk questions are student data privacy, copyright in uploaded readings, and the accuracy of the tutor's answers. Student questions and transcripts are personal data, so the institution must control where they are stored and who can see them. Uploading a published textbook or journal article may exceed what a course reading licence allows, so instructors often use only materials they wrote or that are openly licensed. The tutor can state a wrong fact or method with confidence, so the instructor remains responsible for reviewing logs and correcting errors, and students are typically told the tutor is not an official source of course policy.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Course-specific tutors are moving from single chat windows to tools that can follow a student across a term, remember past mistakes, and adjust practice problems to the student's level. They are also being connected to assignment rubrics so they can give feedback that matches the instructor's grading criteria without assigning marks. The next step is likely tighter integration with learning management systems, where the tutor can see which readings a student has opened and which quiz questions they missed, but this raises new questions about surveillance and student autonomy. The value will depend less on the model and more on how carefully the instructor curates the course material and reviews the tutor's output.
